response.passage: Rohan runs a small wooden toy shop where he crafts identical triangular decorative pieces for wall hangings. To ensure quality, he uses a template. He cuts two wooden triangles, Triangle A and Triangle B. Even when Rohan flips Triangle B over or rotates it to fit a different corner, it remains perfectly congruent to Triangle A because its size and shape are unchanged. A customer once asked if two triangles are congruent just because they have the same three angles. Rohan explained that AAA only proves the triangles have the same shape, not the same size, so they are not necessarily congruent. He then showed two triangles where he measured two sides and the included angle between them. He explained that this SAS criterion works because the angle is trapped between the equal sides. Finally, he pointed to a shared side between two joined triangles, noting that this single side counts as an equal part for both triangles simultaneously. He emphasized that congruence is about exact equality of corresponding parts, not just similarity. By carefully matching vertices in the correct order, he ensures that every piece he sells is a perfect match, proving that congruence requires specific criteria like SAS or ASA, rather than just matching any three parts randomly.
response.summary: Rohan explains that congruence requires identical size and shape, not just similar angles. He demonstrates that specific criteria like SAS are necessary to prove triangles are perfectly equal.
